items.title: Z.ai releases GLM-5.4, its first loop transformer model using weight-shared layers for deeper networks without increasing parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.summary:
Chinese AI lab Z.ai has launched GLM-5.4, its first model employing a loop transformer architecture where a group of weight-shared layers iteratively refines hidden states to deepen the network without adding parameters. This approach follows a similar recent development by Thinking Machines Lab with their Inkling 2 Mini model.

GLM-5.4 is currently accessible only via Z.ai's Coding Plan subscription API, which shares an OpenAI-compatible interface with the regular API. Early tests show that GLM-5.4 produces output quality comparable to its predecessor GLM-5.3 and similar to models from OpenAI and Anthropic, marking a stylistic shift from earlier GLM versions. Community plugins are being updated to support the new model as it gains adoption.

items.originalSummary:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.

It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.

I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.

Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.

It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.

I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

items.title: Researchers introduce Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards to improve demographic fidelity in human-behavior simulation by large language models, reducing distributional divergence on OpinionQA dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards for Human-Behavior Simulation
items.summary:
Researchers propose Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards (DVR), a reinforcement learning approach designed to align large language model-generated survey responses with human demographic distributions. DVR aims to balance individual response accuracy with population-level distributional fidelity, addressing limitations of prior methods that either focus on exact matches or ignore demographic variation.

Evaluated on the OpinionQA dataset, DVR reduced Jensen-Shannon divergence by 34.5% in-distribution and 14.6% on held-out questions compared to accuracy-only rewards, while maintaining per-response accuracy. The study highlights that low distributional divergence alone is insufficient to ensure demographic fidelity, emphasizing the need to jointly evaluate accuracy, distributional fit, and demographic structure in human-behavior simulation models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.28048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents in social-science research. A useful simulator should predict individual responses, reproduce population response distributions, and capture demographic differences. Common training approaches struggle to balance these goals: exact-match rewards encourage the model to concentrate on the most frequent human response, which is contradictory to the goal of distributional alignment. Meanwhile, aggregate distribution matching can look good even when demographic information is ignored. To this end, we introduce Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards (DVR), a reinforcement-learning reward that uses demographic group distribution gaps to guide individual responses, designed by aligning policy generated frequencies with human response frequencies within each question-group margins. We evaluate the method using the OpinionQA dataset and find that comparing with accuracy-only RLVR, DVR preserves per-response accuracy while reducing JSD by 34.5% in-distribution and 14.6% on held-out questions, with higher DPC point estimates on both splits. Comparing KL-SFT with the demographics-blind marginal further shows that low JSD is insufficient to establish fidelity to population heterogeneity, highlighting that accuracy, distributional fit, and demographic structure should be evaluated together.

items.title: Researchers introduce TradeoffBench to expose silent value completion failures in multi-criterion LLM evaluation, finding frequent unsupported winner selections and proposing identified-first evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Rubrics Do Not Decide: Silent Value Completion in LLM Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers identify a common issue in large language model (LLM) evaluation where multi-criterion judges issue strict verdicts without specifying trade-off premises, a problem termed silent value completion. They introduce TradeoffBench, a benchmark that separates rule execution from response scoring, revealing that non-reasoning judges often select unsupported winners in 9% to 81% of conflicts despite passing dominance and equality controls. Reasoning-enabled judges reduce violations but still struggle with omitted trade-offs and divergent scoring.

The study analyzes GPT-6.1-sol and other reasoning judges on datasets with unspecified or explicit trade-offs, finding that many strict verdicts omit necessary completion premises. Human-score audits show that averaging peer scores increases disagreement significantly, and declared partial trade-offs improve coverage but introduce some disagreement. The authors conclude that reliable LLM judging requires separate auditing, specification support, explicit trade-offs, and human target agreement to ensure consistent and justified evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.28940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-criterion LLM judges often evaluate responses without specifying how conflicting criteria resolve, leaving the winner undetermined even under exact criterion scores. Issuing a strict verdict without declaring the required trade-off premise constitutes silent value completion. We introduce TradeoffBench to isolate this failure by separating rule execution from response scoring. On authoritative criterion vectors, six open-weight non-reasoning judges pass all dominance and equality controls yet pick unsupported winners on 9%-81% of 1,345 conflicts. All 577 order-stable choices follow an explicitly banned majority rule. Reasoning-enabled configurations drop anonymous-vector violations to 2 in 9,720 judgments under an explicit rule, yet cannot bridge omitted trade-offs or divergent component scoring. On raw TradeoffBench text with unspecified trade-offs, GPT-6.1-sol omits its completion premise in 29.8% of 400 verified conflicts. Even under an explicit rule on four-rater-consensus MultiPref conflicts, four reasoning judges still issue strict verdicts on 16/45 (GPT-6.1-sol) up to 35/46 and 25/29 (open-weight judges) of valid presentations. We propose identified-first evaluation, decoupling specification support, explicit completion, and target agreement. In MultiPref human-score audits, peer-mean substitution raises directional disagreement from 0.6% to 28.8% on 2,707 shared targets. A single-peer ablation confirms a 29.38-point gap on 2,175 targets, ruling out averaging as the cause. In HUMAINE, declared partial trade-offs add 2.5 percentage points of coverage, yet newly decided pairs incur 3.9% disagreement versus 0.9% for Pareto. Reliable LLM judging, therefore, requires auditing, specification support, declared trade-offs, and human target agreement separately.

items.title: Researchers introduce Population-Based Post-Training to improve large language model tuning by training multiple models in parallel with dynamic hyperparameter adjustment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers propose Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT) as a new method for tuning large language models, which trains several models simultaneously and adjusts hyperparameters dynamically through population-based training. PBPT evaluates models periodically, duplicates high performers with perturbed hyperparameters, and replaces low performers, enabling automatic discovery of better training settings.

PBPT outperforms compute-matched groups of independent reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learners on reasoning benchmarks like Enigmata and Nemotron, as well as interactive tool-use environments such as Gaia2 and AppWorld. The approach also recovers from poor initial hyperparameters, improving model performance over the course of training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

items.title: Researchers introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline to evaluate AI coding agents optimizing CPU kernels across evolving Arm architectural extensions including Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
items.summary:
KernelShift is a new benchmarking framework designed to assess how effectively AI coding agents optimize CPU kernels as hardware architectures evolve, focusing on Arm's specialized extensions. The pipeline converts real-world code repositories into benchmark instances and provides environments for agents to optimize code with direct hardware feedback. The study includes 99 kernels from active projects like ncnn and KleidiAI, covering inference workloads from real model executions.

Evaluations show that AI agents outperform auto-vectorized compilers by 2.4 to 19.8 times and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn by up to 2.74 times on established extensions, though they lag behind hand-tuned kernels like KleidiAI. In end-to-end inference of two large language models, agent-generated kernels achieve a 1.3 to 1.6 times speedup over existing fast paths. However, current agents struggle to adapt reliably to newer extensions requiring unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

items.title: Researchers predict which loopholes large language model judges will exploit before reinforcement learning training using exposure and false-positive rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Which Loopholes Get Found? Predicting Reward Hacking of LLM Judges Before RL Training
items.summary:
Researchers studied how policies trained against large language model (LLM) judges can exploit loopholes in the judges' evaluation criteria. They found that the first loophole a policy exploits can be predicted before reinforcement learning (RL) training by measuring each pattern's exposure, defined as the product of the policy's tendency to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate. This prediction held across multiple experiments involving different judges and seeding patterns into fine-tuning data.

The study involved 36 runs with seven judges using a method called GRPO, where patterns were seeded at varying doses in a Latin square design. Results showed that the first exploited loophole consistently had the highest exposure, even when false-positive rates alone did not predict exploitation. Exploitation occurred mainly on difficult prompts where exploiting a loophole provided a significant advantage. The findings suggest that auditing exposure before RL training can identify which loopholes a policy is likely to exploit first, aiding in the design of more robust LLM judges.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.

items.title: Researchers introduce CivilTime-Bench to evaluate large language models' civil-time reasoning, revealing varied accuracy and generalization challenges across seven models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When 1+1 $\neq$ 2: Benchmarking Civil-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark designed to test large language models' ability to reason about civil time, including complexities like daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. They evaluated seven models using over 60,000 training and 10,000 evaluation examples, finding significant variation in zero-shot exact match accuracy and mixed results from contract-aware prompting and few-shot learning.

Fine-tuning improved performance on synthetic data with exact match scores between 74.6% and 86.6%, but models struggled to generalize to human-generated data, achieving only 36.6% to 45.2% accuracy. The benchmark and code have been released to facilitate further research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calendar arithmetic is non-linear. When 1:59 AM + 1 minute occurs during daylight saving spring-forward, the result is 3:00 AM, not 2:00 AM, as the hour is skipped. We introduce CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark for civil-time reasoning covering daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. With 60,011 training and 10,500 evaluation examples under strict output-contract evaluation, we benchmark seven LLMs (six instruction-tuned models and Llama-3.1-8B base) and find: zero-shot exact match varies substantially across models, contract-aware prompting often improves format compliance but yields inconsistent accuracy gains, few-shot in-context learning provides model-dependent improvements, and fine-tuning achieves 74.6--86.6% EM on synthetic evaluation but only 36.6--45.2% on HumanTime-500 for models with valid results on both splits, highlighting substantial limitations in generalization. We release the benchmark and code.

items.title: Researchers audit SWE-Gym coding tasks, find 74% of unsolved tasks have mislabelled tests rejecting correct fixes, and release SWE-Gym-Verified with 1,087 audited tasks and audit pipeline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic audit of SWE-Gym, a reinforcement learning environment for training coding agents, focusing on the correctness of reward labels determined by hidden tests. They found that 74% of tasks never solved by a 9B parameter model contained false negatives where tests rejected correct fixes, compared to 20% for sometimes solved tasks. After repairing or removing mislabelled tasks, models trained on the audited set scored 2.4 to 2.7 points higher on held-out benchmarks than those trained on the original tasks, while simply dropping unsolved tasks did not improve performance.

The study also identified that about a quarter of passing patches were false positives, but adding new tests to catch some of these did not significantly affect evaluation scores. The researchers emphasize that pass rates indicate whether a task yields reward but do not guarantee the reward's correctness, highlighting the need to verify reward labels. To support further research, they released SWE-Gym-Verified, which includes 1,087 audited tasks with execution evidence, training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.30207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

items.title: Researchers propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement to enhance large language models by iteratively refining answers and updating model weights, improving accuracy by nearly 14% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a framework for large language models (LLMs) that improves performance after deployment without labeled data. TT-RSI combines In-Context RSI, which re-solves questions using previous solutions as references, and In-Weight RSI, which distills refinements into the model's weights to surpass initial majority errors and approach an infinite-step refinement limit.

Experiments demonstrate that TT-RSI increases average accuracy by 13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by 4.79% under the same test-time computational budget, suggesting a promising approach for ongoing LLM improvement during inference.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.30965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

items.title: Researchers introduce SMB Bench to evaluate language model agents on acting with delayed consequences in multi-day wholesale operations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
items.summary:
Researchers present SMB Bench, a 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run dataset, to study how language model agents recognize and act on delayed effects of decisions in ongoing business operations. They found that while some models diagnose problems, few change behavior effectively to improve outcomes, highlighting the distinction between diagnosis, action, and business improvement.

Using the open model Qwen3.8-27B, the team trained policies on archived business records to better follow customer-protection commitments and reduce severe losses in unseen test scenarios, though profit gains were uncertain. The study reveals challenges in coordinating decisions over time, as early stocking habits affected reliance on emergency supplies and supplier quality, and connects these insights to a learning method that reuses past decisions and outcomes as training experience.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.28158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

items.summary: This study demonstrates that a shared prompt-refinement method guided by affective and cognitive feedback can enhance agreement with held-out references, improve multi-label classification, and reduce variability in affective generation for educational AI systems without updating executor parameters. The approach was tested using a secondary language model that revised prompts based on discrepancies in affective references and Bloom's taxonomy labels across multiple dialogues and learning outcomes. Results showed reductions in affective error and generation variability alongside significant improvements in classification accuracy, suggesting prompt refinement as a promising technique for adaptive technical instruction, though its impact on workforce learning remains to be evaluated.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.28293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.

items.title: Researchers propose INSEP defense to reduce refusal-direction separability in large language models, mitigating abliteration attacks across eight models from 1B to 14B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
items.summary:
INSEP is a new defense against abliteration, a white-box attack that induces harmful behavior in large language models by projecting out a refusal direction in activation space. The method fine-tunes models to reduce the separability between harmful and benign activations along this direction, weakening the attack's signal while preserving the model's refusal behavior and response quality.

The approach uses adversarial eigendecomposition to identify the most separable prompt subsets and applies a low-rank adapter to reduce their separation. INSEP was benchmarked against six existing defenses under five attacks across eight models from various families, showing top performance on a composite score measuring harm, coherence, directness, over-refusal, and knowledge benchmarks, while maintaining utility. This evaluation represents the largest reported study of abliteration defenses to date.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.28314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate an AI agent that writes new capabilities into pretrained language model weights without backpropagation, improving BIG-Bench Hard scores on Qwen2.5 and Gemma-3 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
items.summary:
Researchers show that an AI agent can enhance pretrained language models by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons within existing layers without using backpropagation or fitting weights to task answers. This method, limited to 50 model passes and without exposure to validation or test data, significantly improves BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) scores for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Gemma-3-1B-it models while maintaining unchanged next-token distributions and identical performance on other benchmarks.
The agent also successfully writes exact multiplication capabilities up to 20 digits, outperforming comparable LoRA methods. The experiments were rigorously controlled with sealed test sets and timestamped manifests, and evaluations confirmed success across multiple subtasks and tests. Some modules showed minor side effects, and a few sessions reached the 12-hour runtime limit without completing a module, indicating areas for further refinement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.28483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.

items.title: Researchers propose DoC framework for early, accurate, and stable conversational diagnosis prediction using defer/commit learning with reinforcement training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DoC: Learning to Defer or Commit for Timely, Accurate, and Stable Conversational Diagnosis Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers introduce DoC, a two-phase framework designed to improve conversational diagnosis prediction by learning when to defer or commit decisions during clinical dialogues. The approach uses iterative commitment-boundary estimation to generate supervision without annotated commitment times, followed by defer-aware supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to optimize timeliness, accuracy, and stability.

Evaluated on EMSDialog and MediTOD datasets, DoC achieves the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7% and 51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error rates (16.4% and 48.3%), demonstrating its effectiveness in making early and reliable diagnostic predictions from ongoing conversations.

Evaluated on EMSDialog and MediTOD datasets, DoC achieves the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7% and 51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error rates (16.4% and 48.3%), demonstrating its effectiveness in making early and reliable diagnostic predictions from ongoing conversations.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational diagnosis prediction requires accurate, early, and stable predictions from ongoing clinical dialogue, yet dialogue-level labels do not specify when to commit. We propose a two-phase framework for learning deferral and diagnosis decisions. First, iterative commitment-boundary estimation constructs Defer/diagnosis supervision without annotated commitment times. Second, Defer-aware supervised fine-tuning initializes a policy, refined through reinforcement learning with trajectory-level rewards for timeliness, first-commit accuracy, and post-commit stability. On EMSDialog and MediTOD, DoC commits early, achieving the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7%/51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error overall (16.4%/48.3%).

items.title: VeriLogic introduces reinforcement learning on verifiable logical reasoning traces, improving reasoning accuracy by decomposing and verifying intermediate steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VeriLogic: Reinforcement Learning over Verifiable Logical Reasoning Traces
items.summary: VeriLogic presents a reinforcement learning framework that treats logical reasoning as a sequence of verifiable intermediate steps rather than a single outcome, enabling process-level verification and targeted learning. The approach organizes reasoning into a "Grounding - Optimization - Refinement" pipeline, which grounds reasoning in explicit states, optimizes policies using verifier feedback, and iteratively refines reasoning based on proof diagnostics. Experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, with average accuracy gains of 6.39% on Qwen3 and 5.00% on Llama-3.1, highlighting the benefits of making reasoning traces verifiable and learnable beyond final-answer supervision.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Logical reasoning derives conclusions from premises through explicit intermediate inference steps, providing a natural basis for process-level verification and supervision. However, existing learning methods often rely on response-level outcome signals, which overlook heterogeneous correctness within the reasoning trace: a correct answer may contain invalid reasoning, while valid intermediate steps may also appear in an incorrect response. To address this issue, we introduce Reinforcement Learning on Verifiable Logical Reasoning (VeriLogic), which turns internal reasoning traces into explicit and verifiable learning objects. Rather than treating a response as an indivisible learning unit, VeriLogic decomposes logical reasoning into explicit intermediate judgments, proofs, and final decisions, and organizes them into a unified "Grounding - Optimization - Refinement" pipeline: (1) Verification-Grounded Reasoning Environment Construction grounds logical reasoning into explicit intermediate states and formally checkable proof obligations, making the internal reasoning process accessible to verification and learning; (2) Logical Structured Policy Optimization learns from verifier feedback through complementary global and local rewards, jointly optimizing the overall reasoning outcome while providing targeted optimization signals to different intermediate reasoning paths; and (3) Verifier-Guided Iterative Refinement acts on verifier feedback by leveraging proof states and error messages to iteratively diagnose and repair failed reasoning. Experiments on six logical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over strong baselines, with average improvements of 6.39% and 5.00% on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1. These results highlight the value of making logical reasoning traces verifiable, learnable, and refinable beyond final-answer supervision.

items.title: Researchers propose Direct Feedback Policy Optimization, a single-trajectory reinforcement learning method that improves task resolution rates for AI coding agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Direct Feedback Policy Optimization for AI Coding Agents
items.summary: Researchers introduce Direct Feedback Policy Optimization (DFPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm designed for AI coding agents that generate, modify, and validate code through multi-turn interactions. Unlike existing methods relying on sparse terminal rewards or repeated sampling, DFPO trains directly from a single trajectory, enabling better assessment of intermediate decisions' impact on task outcomes. DFPO demonstrates higher task resolution rates compared to Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GSPO) when tested with matched base models and execution environments.

DFPO demonstrates higher task resolution rates compared to Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GSPO) when tested with matched base models and execution environments.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents generate, modify, and validate code through multi-turn interactions. Existing reinforcement learning methods often rely on sparse terminal rewards, making it difficult to assess how intermediate decisions affect task outcomes, and group-relative methods also require repeated sampling for each task. We propose Direct Feedback Policy Optimization (DFPO), a single-trajectory reinforcement learning algorithm that trains directly from a single trajectory. DFPO achieves higher task resolution rates than GSPO under matched base models and execution harnesses.

items.title: NoeVera system integrates knowledge and experiments to optimize large language model serving configurations, achieving near-optimal results with fewer simulations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
items.summary:
NoeVera is an agentic system designed to improve optimization of large language model (LLM) serving by creating a persistent knowledge base from papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results. It uses decision-aware retrieval and role-specific agents to guide experiments and refine knowledge, reducing the number of simulator calls needed to approach optimal configurations.

In tests across four serving scenarios, NoeVera achieved configurations within 5% of the optimum using a median of 6-7 simulator calls, outperforming Bayesian optimization and knowledge-free agents. Its configurations improved throughput by about 30% on A100 GPUs while meeting latency goals. The system also demonstrated lower over-generalization in evidence reuse and scored significantly higher on a held-out benchmark compared to other agents, maintaining advantages even when baselines used NoeVera's prompts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

items.title: Researchers identify latent confidence directions in large reasoning models that predict and steer backtracking behavior during answer proposals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers studied three 32-billion-parameter reasoning models and found that despite reaching correct answers, models often backtrack and propose multiple answers, leading to long reasoning traces. They hypothesized that models maintain an internal representation of uncertainty and extracted a linear latent confidence direction from verbalized confidence signals that correlates with backtracking behavior.

By steering this latent confidence direction, the researchers modulated the length of response traces and the number of answer proposals with minimal impact on accuracy. Applying this approach from the start of generation also shortened traces and influenced the linguistic confidence of proposals. The study reveals a close relationship between a model's internal confidence representation and its tendency to backtrack or commit to answers during reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.29265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.

items.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.

items.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

items.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.

items.title: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.

items.title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.29954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).

items.title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination
items.summary: arXiv:2611.30639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.

items.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace? [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.31015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.

items.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
items.summary: arXiv:2611.31113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $\tau = 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($\beta_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

items.title: Token Noise and the Illusion of Preference: A Shapley Value Framework for Auditing LLM-Simulated Choice Experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Token Noise and the Illusion of Preference: A Shapley Value Framework for Auditing LLM-Simulated Choice Experiments
items.summary: arXiv:2404.01332v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human respondents in choice experiments, yet their answers depend on the exact tokens of a prompt rather than on the offered products alone. I show that invisible characters, blank lines, or minor wording changes shift or reverse simulated choice probabilities. This sensitivity, which I term token noise, creates an illusion of preference and exposes studies to prompt hacking. I introduce a Shapley value audit that divides a model's choice response among the pieces of its prompt and reads each share beside the effect of removing that piece. The edit game divides the effect of several wording and formatting changes beside an actual price change. The word game divides a prompt's response across its words or tokens and summarizes the credit earned by the product attributes as the attribute share. Across four open-weight models and three product categories, wording and formatting edits could rival a substantive price change, while product attributes consistently received a minority of the word-level credit, sometimes less than the answer instruction. Framing cues could take credit from the very price they emphasized and frequently vanished or reversed across equivalent wordings of the question. A persona (even a bare statement that the respondent is a consumer) also shifted choice probabilities and the attributes' credit. Declared with its "players," reference, scale, and uncertainty, my audit separates what a simulated respondent prefers from how the question was asked, the distinction a study must draw before it reads a simulated choice as a preference.

items.title: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2501.14851v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Logical reasoning is a critical component of Large Language Models (LLMs), and substantial research efforts in recent years have aimed to enhance their deductive reasoning abilities. However, existing deductive reasoning benchmarks suffer from significant constraints that restrict their utility, i.e., the lack of task complexity, the presence of prior knowledge as a confounder, and superficial error analysis. To address these deficiencies, we introduce JustLogic, a synthetically generated benchmark for evaluating deduction in propositional logic. Within this fragment, JustLogic is (i) complex, capable of generating a diverse range of linguistic patterns, vocabulary, and argument structures, (ii) prior knowledge independent, substantially reducing the advantage of models possessing prior knowledge so that questions are answerable from the given premises alone, and (iii) capable of in-depth error analysis on the heterogeneous effects of proof size and argument form on model accuracy. Our experimental results on JustLogic reveal that (i) several state-of-the-art (SOTA) reasoning LLMs score above the human average on JustLogic, although only DeepSeek R1's margin is significant on the matched items after correction for multiple comparisons, and (ii) the evaluated non-reasoning models score below the human average. Given the small human study (18 participants, seven questions each), these comparisons are indicative. All code and data are available at https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic

items.title: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Chain-of-Thought Fails, the Solution Hides in the Hidden States
items.summary: arXiv:2604.23351v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether intermediate reasoning is computationally useful or merely explanatory depends on whether chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens contain task-solving information. We present a mechanistic causal analysis of CoT on GSM8K using activation patching: transferring token-level hidden states from an arithmetic CoT generation to a direct-answer run for the same question, then measuring the effect on final-answer accuracy. Across models, patching can elicit generations that lead to correct answers, revealing that individual CoT hidden states can encode sufficient task-solving information even when the original CoT trace is incorrect. This information is more prevalent in correct than incorrect CoT runs and is unevenly distributed across tokens, concentrating in mid-to-late layers and appearing earlier in the reasoning trace. Moreover, patching from language tokens such as verbs and entities more frequently elicits correct reasoning traces, whereas patches from mathematical tokens more often produce answer-proximal generations that rarely succeed. Further analysis shows that earlier CoT tokens concentrate recoverable information, while later ones require broader search to find the correct answer. Together, these findings show that CoT encodes recoverable, token-level task-solving information, revealing how arithmetic reasoning is represented, accessed, and disrupted.

items.title: Post-training is (Massive) Supervised Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-training is (Massive) Supervised Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2606.07527v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The prevailing paradigm for training LLMs has evolved to rely on a massive post-training phase consisting of SFT and RL. In this position paper, we argue that this methodology effectively marks a reversion to the ``pre-train then fine-tune'' approach of the BERT era, explicitly tailoring models to the desired behaviors and specific benchmarks on which they are evaluated. We begin with a historical overview of LLMs, describing the different phases of the LLM evolution. We argue that the current landscape is remarkably similar to the early days of LLMs, where task performance heavily relied on fitting the models to in-distribution datasets. To empirically demonstrate this, we compare pre-trained models to randomly initialized ones, by fine-tuning both variants on modern reasoning datasets and evaluating them on competitive math and code benchmarks. We show that models post-trained from scratch yield highly non-trivial performance. Our findings suggest that current post-training methodologies function primarily as a distribution-fitting mechanism. We finish by positing that developing generally capable models and systems requires moving beyond extensive post-training for predefined behaviors, shifting instead toward training procedures where models ``learn how to learn''.

items.title: FOCUS & RePAIR: Mitigating Text Degeneration via Token-Level Guidance for Pruned Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FOCUS & RePAIR: Mitigating Text Degeneration via Token-Level Guidance for Pruned Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2608.26676v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pruning is a practical approach to compress large language models (LLMs), but it can amplify text degeneration, especially repetition loops, even when perplexity and task accuracy remain largely unchanged. In this work, we present a token-level analysis of this failure mode by viewing decoding as a dynamical process that enters and persists in a small set of recurrent contexts. Our analysis decomposes degeneration into loop entry risk and loop persistence, and shows that persistence is controlled by the escape mass assigned to plausible alternatives within the token sampling set. Motivated by these findings, we propose two token-level guidance objectives for post-pruning fine-tuning. FOCUS reweights distillation toward high-confidence teacher regions to suppress leakage, while RePAIR uses onset-centered positive/negative continuation pairs with a margin loss to promote plausible alternatives and prevent early commitment to repetition loops. Experiments on open-ended continuation and instruction-based generation show that both methods consistently reduce repetition and improve generation quality.

items.title: Sparse Readout Prism: Explaining Logit-Lens Scores in Features Instead of Tokens
items.originalTitle: Sparse Readout Prism: Explaining Logit-Lens Scores in Features Instead of Tokens
items.summary: arXiv:2609.01936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lens methods interpret intermediate hidden states by transporting them to the final layer and decoding them through the unembedding matrix into token scores. Fitted lenses learn their transport map from a training corpus. We find that changing only the corpus can change token rankings for the same hidden state; we call this corpus conditionality. To test whether two differently fitted lenses share unembedding features, we introduce Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), which learns these features by reconstructing each unembedding row as a sparse combination of them. SRP measures each feature's contribution to a lens score without changing the lens's transport. Across six models, SRP reconstructs logit differences more accurately than geometric baselines. On Ministral-3-8B, English and Chinese Jacobian lenses disagree on the top token for all prompts at one layer in both comparisons, versus at most 10% for same-language refits at that layer. On Qwen3.5-9B, disagreement reaches 87% between English and German Jacobian lenses and 94% between English and Chinese ridge lenses. At one layer, SRP finds the same dominant feature in the two lenses' top-token scores for 81% of prompts with English and German Jacobian lenses on Qwen and up to 78% with English and Chinese Jacobian lenses on Ministral.

items.title: Cross-modal RAG: Sub-dimensional Text-to-Image Retrieval-Augmented Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-modal RAG: Sub-dimensional Text-to-Image Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2505.21956v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-to-image generation increasingly demands access to domain-specific, fine-grained, and rapidly evolving knowledge that pretrained models cannot fully capture, necessitating the integration of retrieval methods. Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods attempt to address this by retrieving globally relevant images, but they fail when no single image contains all desired elements from a complex user query. We propose Cross-modal RAG, a novel framework that decomposes both queries and images into sub-dimensional components, enabling subquery-aware retrieval and generation. Our method introduces a hybrid retrieval strategy, combining a sub-dimensional sparse retriever with a dense retriever, to identify a Pareto-optimal set of images, each contributing complementary aspects of the query. During generation, a multimodal large language model is guided to selectively condition on relevant visual features aligned to specific subqueries for subquery-aware image synthesis. Extensive experiments on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, WikiArt, CUB, and ImageNet-LT demonstrate that Cross-modal RAG significantly outperforms existing baselines in the retrieval and further contributes to generation quality, while maintaining high efficiency.
